learning.topic.digitalPrivacy.title: What is Digital Privacy?
learning.topic.digitalPrivacy.tagline: Privacy isn't about hiding. It's about having control.
learning.topic.digitalPrivacy.summary: Digital privacy means deciding who can access information about you, when they can access it, and why.
learning.topic.digitalPrivacy.situation: You browse websites, send messages, shop online and use social media every day. Most of the time, you don't think about what information is being collected.
learning.topic.digitalPrivacy.problem: Many people believe privacy only matters if they have something to hide. As a result, they often reveal far more information than they intended.
learning.topic.digitalPrivacy.reality: Many online interactions can create traces. Websites, apps and service providers collect different kinds of information about your activity. Privacy is about understanding this process and making informed choices.
learning.topic.digitalPrivacy.solution: You don't need to disappear from the Internet. You only need to understand what information you share and decide when it's worth sharing.
learning.topic.digitalPrivacy.illustrati: A cat looks into a mirror and sees a silhouette made from icons representing messages, photos, locations, accounts and other pieces of digital information.
learning.topic.digitalFootprint.title: Your Digital Footprint
learning.topic.digitalFootprint.tagline: The internet remembers more than you do.
learning.topic.digitalFootprint.summary: Your digital footprint is the collection of traces created by your activity online.
learning.topic.digitalFootprint.situatio: You search for information, visit websites, like posts, install apps and create accounts. Each action feels small and separate.
learning.topic.digitalFootprint.problem: It is difficult to see the complete picture. Information shared at different times and in different places can be connected to reveal more about you than any single action suggests.
learning.topic.digitalFootprint.reality: Some traces are intentional, such as public posts. Others are created automatically, including technical data, activity records and identifiers. Together they form a digital footprint that can persist for years.
learning.topic.digitalFootprint.solution: Pause before sharing, review old accounts and permissions, and remove information you no longer want online. You cannot erase every trace, but you can decide which new ones you leave.
learning.topic.digitalFootprint.illustra: A person's silhouette inside a digital card is connected to location, message, photo, profile and reaction icons.
learning.topic.whyCare.title: Why Should I Care?
learning.topic.whyCare.tagline: You have nothing to hide. You still close your curtains.
learning.topic.whyCare.summary: Privacy protects everyday life, not only secrets.
learning.topic.whyCare.situation: You share photos with friends, talk to family, search for health information and manage your money online. None of these actions is suspicious or unusual.
learning.topic.whyCare.problem: The phrase 'I have nothing to hide' makes privacy sound useful only for people doing something wrong. It ignores the difference between choosing to share and being observed without your knowledge.
learning.topic.whyCare.reality: Information changes meaning when it is combined, taken out of context or used later for a different purpose. Privacy gives you space to think, communicate and make ordinary decisions without constant observation.
learning.topic.whyCare.solution: Treat privacy as a normal boundary. Ask why information is requested, share only what is necessary and choose services that give you meaningful control over your data.
learning.topic.whyCare.illustration.alt: Digital traces from everyday life pass through a prism and form a detailed silhouette of a person.
learning.topic.publicWifi.title: Public Wi-Fi
learning.topic.publicWifi.tagline: The coffee is free. The network might not be.
learning.topic.publicWifi.summary: Public Wi-Fi is convenient, but you do not control the network or always know who operates it.
learning.topic.publicWifi.situation: You are waiting at an airport or sitting in a café. Your phone finds a free network with a familiar name, so you connect and continue using the internet as usual.
learning.topic.publicWifi.problem: A network name is not proof that the network is trustworthy. Someone can create a convincing fake access point, and other people connected nearby may try to observe or manipulate traffic.
learning.topic.publicWifi.reality: HTTPS protects the contents of most modern web connections, so public Wi-Fi does not automatically expose everything you do. Risks still remain: fake login pages, insecure apps, misleading network names and devices configured to share more than intended.
learning.topic.publicWifi.solution: Confirm the official network name, do not ignore unexpected login pages or certificate warnings, keep sharing disabled and prefer mobile data for sensitive tasks. A trusted VPN can reduce some network-level exposure, but it cannot make phishing sites safe.
learning.topic.passwords.title: Passwords
learning.topic.passwords.tagline: One leaked password should not unlock your whole life.
learning.topic.passwords.summary: A password protects one account only when it is strong, unique and stored safely.
learning.topic.passwords.situation: You create accounts constantly. Remembering a different password for every service feels impossible, so reusing one familiar password seems practical.
learning.topic.passwords.problem: When one service is breached, attackers test exposed email and password combinations elsewhere. A password stolen from a low-priority account can give them access to your email, shopping or social accounts.
learning.topic.passwords.reality: The biggest risk is often reuse, not whether a password contains one more symbol. Long, unique passwords limit the damage of a breach. A password manager can generate and store them so you do not need to remember each one.
learning.topic.passwords.solution: Use a unique password for every important account, starting with your email. Store them in a trusted password manager and enable multi-factor authentication. If a service reports a breach, change the affected password immediately wherever it was reused.
learning.topic.smsAuth.title: SMS Authentication
learning.topic.smsAuth.tagline: The familiar option is not always the strongest.
learning.topic.smsAuth.summary: SMS codes add protection, but your phone number is not a security key that only you can control.
learning.topic.smsAuth.situation: You enter a password and receive a six-digit code by text message. Because the code arrives on your phone, the login feels protected by something only you possess.
learning.topic.smsAuth.problem: A phone number depends on mobile networks, account recovery procedures and the security of your mobile operator account. If someone gains control of the number, they may also receive authentication messages intended for you.
learning.topic.smsAuth.reality: SMS authentication is usually safer than using only a password, and it may be the only second-factor option a service provides. Authenticator apps avoid relying on the phone number, although their codes can still be phished. Passkeys and compatible physical security keys can provide phishing-resistant authentication.
learning.topic.smsAuth.solution: Keep SMS verification enabled when the alternative is password-only access. For important accounts, prefer a passkey, authenticator app or security key when available. Protect your mobile operator account with a strong password and an additional account PIN.

learning.topic.socialMedia.title: Social Media
learning.topic.socialMedia.tagline: You are not only sharing with friends.
learning.topic.socialMedia.summary: A post can reveal more through its audience, timing and context than through its text alone.
learning.topic.socialMedia.situation: You share a photo, tag a location, react to a post or follow a new account. Each action feels small and is usually intended for friends or a familiar community.
learning.topic.socialMedia.problem: A post may reach a wider audience and remain accessible far longer than expected. Public profiles, screenshots, resharing and changing platform policies can move information beyond the people you originally chose.
learning.topic.socialMedia.reality: Platforms can learn from both published content and patterns such as what you view, when you are active and who you interact with. Privacy settings reduce exposure, but they cannot control copies made by other people or every use of platform data.
learning.topic.socialMedia.solution: Review your audience and old posts, disable unnecessary location access and avoid publishing details that could expose routines or answers to account-recovery questions. Before posting, assume the content may eventually reach someone outside the intended audience.
A single post spreads through expanding circles and reaches an increasing number of people.
learning.topic.messagingApps.title: Messaging Apps
learning.topic.messagingApps.tagline: A private message is more than encrypted text.
learning.topic.messagingApps.summary: Messaging apps protect conversations in different ways: encrypting the contents does not always protect the surrounding metadata.
learning.topic.messagingApps.situation: You send personal messages, photos, documents and voice notes throughout the day. The apps look similar, so it is easy to assume they provide the same level of privacy.
learning.topic.messagingApps.problem: Encryption may protect message contents while other information remains available, such as your phone number, contacts, communication times or cloud backups. A secure conversation can also be exposed through an unlocked device.
learning.topic.messagingApps.reality: End-to-end encryption means only the participants' devices should be able to read message contents. It does not automatically hide every piece of metadata, protect every backup or prevent recipients from copying what you send.
learning.topic.messagingApps.solution: Prefer messaging apps with end-to-end encryption enabled by default, understand which identifiers they require and check how backups work. Protect the device itself, verify a contact's identity when needed and treat disappearing messages as an extra precaution, not a guarantee.
learning.topic.messagingApps.illustratio: A protected message is surrounded by connected metadata: identity, time, location and device.
learning.topic.vpn.title: VPN
learning.topic.vpn.tagline: Useful protection, not an invisibility cloak.
learning.topic.vpn.summary: A VPN changes who can observe your network connection, but it does not make every online action anonymous or safe.
learning.topic.vpn.situation: You connect to a VPN and see a different IP address. Websites still load normally, so it can feel as though your entire online identity has disappeared.
learning.topic.vpn.problem: Marketing often presents a VPN as complete privacy protection. This can create the false impression that it protects you from phishing, account-based tracking, malware and the consequences of information you share voluntarily.
learning.topic.vpn.reality: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN provider and, in many situations, hides from the local network which sites and services you connect to. The VPN provider becomes a trusted intermediary, while websites can still recognize logged-in accounts, cookies and browser characteristics.
learning.topic.vpn.solution: Choose a reputable provider that is transparent about its ownership, policies and limitations. A VPN is especially useful on networks you do not control, but combine it with HTTPS, safe browsing, updated devices and thoughtful privacy settings.
learning.topic.vpn.illustration.alt: A protected VPN tunnel connects a user to the internet across a gap between two sides.
learning.topic.privacyToolkit.title: Building Your Privacy Toolkit
learning.topic.privacyToolkit.tagline: Privacy is a practice, not a single product.
learning.topic.privacyToolkit.summary: A good toolkit combines a few reliable habits with tools chosen for your actual risks.
learning.topic.privacyToolkit.situation: After learning about digital risks, you find long lists of apps, settings and products that promise protection. Trying to adopt everything at once quickly becomes exhausting.
learning.topic.privacyToolkit.problem: A complicated setup is difficult to maintain and may protect against threats that do not matter to you while leaving basic weaknesses unresolved.
learning.topic.privacyToolkit.reality: Privacy has no universal configuration. A traveller, a small-business owner and a person facing harassment have different priorities. Reliable basics usually create more value than advanced tools used incorrectly.
learning.topic.privacyToolkit.solution: Start with unique passwords, secure account-recovery methods, device updates and multi-factor authentication. Then review app permissions, communication methods, network connections and the information you publish. Add a new tool only when you understand which problem it solves and what it cannot protect you from.
learning.topic.privacyToolkit.illustrati: Several privacy tools surround a central shield, with one open space showing that the toolkit can be adapted to personal needs.

learning.category.takingControl.descript: Choose practical habits and tools that match your real privacy needs.
